alt: A band with three zones. On the left, statements that need no defence, such as “Social media exists.” On the right, claims too vast to defend, such as “This policy will solve all of society’s problems.” In the middle, the defensible zone: “Social media has made teenagers better informed but less able to concentrate.”
caption: A good thesis needs defending and can be defended in the space available.

alt: Six crossed-out cards with examples: an announcement (“In this essay I will discuss pollution”), a fact, a restated prompt, a vague evaluation, an unconnected list of devices, and an overreach that cannot be defended.
caption: A thesis is a position, not a plan, a fact, a restatement or a list.

after: ## Thesis formulas that work (and the danger of formulas)
alt: Four scaffolds built from labelled blocks: claim plus reason; concession plus claim; claim plus qualification; and for rhetorical analysis, “[Writer] uses [strategies] to [accomplish purpose] for [audience]”, with “to” highlighted as the key word.
caption: Use scaffolds to draft; in analysis, the key word is “to”: say what the choices accomplish.

after: ## Revising a weak thesis: four questions
alt: A cycle of four questions around a working thesis: could a reasonable person disagree, is it specific, does it say why, and can I defend it in the time and space I have? Each comes with its fix.
caption: Arguable, specific, reasoned and the right size: test and revise in a loop.

after: ## Worked example 1: from topic to thesis
alt: The vague draft “City centres and cars are a big problem today” becomes a thesis built from a position (close city centres to private cars), a qualification (exceptions for residents and deliveries) and a reason (air quality and pedestrian safety outweigh the inconvenience). Four ticks confirm it is arguable, specific, focused and responsive.
caption: Take a position, add a reason, add a qualification, then test it.

after: ## Worked example 2: a rhetorical analysis thesis
alt: The model thesis on the Gettysburg Address split into labelled parts: the situation (“By stressing that the living cannot add...”), the strategies (humility, repetition and a turn to “us the living”), the key word “to”, and what the choices accomplish (a memorial becomes a call to continue the work). Below, a weak thesis only lists devices.
caption: An analysis thesis says what the choices accomplish, not just which choices exist.
